title: ResizeObserver: Depth-Order Measurement and Loop Limit Guard
prerequisites: DOM layout and CSS box model
Understanding of the event loop and microtasks

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Imagine a tailor who measures every customer's suit and adjusts it to fit. If the tailor's tape measure were to change size whenever he measured someone, he would never finish — every measurement would make the next one different. So the shop has a strict rule: measure everyone in a set order, and if a measurement changes someone's size again, you may only do a couple of fix-up rounds before you stop and say 'that's as good as it gets'. ResizeObserver is that tailor with the same rule: it measures elements, applies sizes, and if the sizes keep changing, it stops after a few rounds to avoid an endless loop.
progressiveExplaining.junior: ResizeObserver reports when an element's content-box or border-box size changes. const ro = new ResizeObserver((entries) => { for (const e of entries) { console.log(e.contentRect.width); } }); ro.observe(el);. Unlike window resize events, it observes individual elements and fires after layout settles, with an array of ResizeObserverEntry (target + contentRect + borderBoxSize/contentBoxSize). Useful for responsive components, canvas sizing, and text-overflow clamping. Call ro.disconnect() when done. Entries are delivered once per layout pass, batched; the API is built to avoid infinite feedback when you resize elements inside the callback.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, ResizeObserver delivers notifications after layout, once per frame, batched per observed element. If a callback resizes an element, that triggers another layout pass and a re-delivery; the spec guards against infinite loops by allowing only a bounded number of resize processing passes per frame (the 'loop limit'). Elements are processed in depth order (tree order) so a parent's resize is delivered before its children. contentRect gives content-box geometry; contentBoxSize/borderBoxSize give per-axis boxes with device-pixel precision. This makes it the reliable primitive for element-level responsive behavior, unlike window resize + manual measurement.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The engine keeps a set of observed targets with their last-known sizes. After layout, it computes the new sizes; any change marks the entry for delivery. Delivery happens in the rendering steps ('broadcast active resize observations'): entries are grouped by depth order and passed to the callback synchronously within that step. If the callback mutates sizes, the engine re-runs layout and repeats; the loop limit (spec: 2 processing rounds per update) forces an 'error' event on the ResizeObserver (delivered as a task) when repeated resizing prevents convergence, so the page does not hang. This is why infinite loops are prevented deterministically rather than by heuristics.

rosettaStone.react: ResizeObserver is the modern replacement for window-resize-driven layout in React components (resize-detector, react-resize-observer).
rosettaStone.angular: Angular apps can wrap ResizeObserver in directives; @angular/cdk's Layout module historically used window resize, moving to IO/RO where possible.
rosettaStone.vue: vueuse's useResizeObserver exposes it as a composable; element-level responsive logic fits Composition API nicely.
rosettaStone.svelte: Svelte actions make ResizeObserver attachment declarative: use:resize creates the observer on mount and cleans up on unmount.

codeComparison.title: window.resize + manual measurement vs ResizeObserver
codeComparison.summary: Window resize events miss element-level changes and need manual measurement; ResizeObserver observes the element itself with batched delivery after layout.

legacyOrBad.label: window.resize listener + manual measure
legacyOrBad.snippet: window.addEventListener('resize', () => { const w = el.offsetWidth; render(w); }); // ❌ OLD: only fires on window resize, forces layout read

modernOrGood.label: ResizeObserver on the element
modernOrGood.snippet:
const ro = new ResizeObserver(entries => { render(entries[0].contentRect.width); });
ro.observe(el); // ✅ NEW: observes the element, batched, after layout

interviewGotchas.question: What happens if you resize an element inside a ResizeObserver callback — how does the browser avoid an infinite loop?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This is the defining design question of ResizeObserver — interviewers want the loop-limit mechanism and the depth-order processing rule, not just 'don't resize in the callback'.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Resizing an element inside the callback triggers another layout pass and another delivery. To prevent infinite feedback, the spec defines a bounded resize processing loop: per rendering update, the engine runs at most two processing passes. If after the limit an observation still reports a size change, the engine does not keep looping; it queues an error event (a 'ResizeObserver loop limit exceeded' error delivered as a task) and stops further resizing for that cycle. Elements are processed in depth order (parents before children), so a parent resize that changes child sizes is delivered coherently. This deterministic guard is why the API is safe to use for self-resizing components (e.g. canvas fit-to-container).
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'just don't resize inside the callback'. Self-resizing is a legitimate pattern; the loop limit makes it bounded rather than infinite. Another trap: assuming the error is thrown synchronously — it is reported asynchronously as an error event, so it can be missed in tests. Candidates who explain the two-pass limit and the error event demonstrate understanding of the API's core contract.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the difference between contentRect and contentBoxSize/borderBoxSize, and why does depth-order processing matter?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests precise knowledge of the entry structure and the ordering semantics that prevent cascading measurement bugs in real layouts.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: contentRect is the content-box rectangle (x, y, width, height) in CSS pixels, but it is computed relative to the element's padding box origin and can be lossy for subpixel or non-rectangular layouts. contentBoxSize and borderBoxSize are arrays of ResizeObserverSize objects ({ inlineSize, blockSize }) that preserve device-pixel precision and respect writing modes. Depth-order processing means the engine broadcasts entries parents-first: a parent's size change is delivered before its children, so child observations already reflect the parent's updated size — preventing the classic 'child measured before parent resized' bug. Using borderBoxSize when you care about the full box (borders included) is the recommended precise read.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'contentRect is always the right measurement'. It is deprecated-by-preference in the spec for subpixel precision and has confusing x/y origin semantics. Another trap: assuming entries arrive in observation order — they arrive in depth order per the spec, so relying on insertion order for layout logic breaks. Candidates who cite contentBoxSize/borderBoxSize and depth-order broadcasting show real mastery.
